case_studies.title: LLM2Jev: LLMs Are Already Jev-Style Decision Models -- When and How to Fine-Tune Them
case_studies.abstract: Jev-style decision models return categorical probability distributions over predefined options without generating free-form text, enabling software systems to act on their outputs directly. In this work, we investigate the extent to which general-purpose LLMs already possess this capability out of the box, and when fine-tuning is actually necessary. We present LLM2Jev, an architecture-preserving framework that extracts calibrated decisions directly from next-token probabilities over bracketed numeric identifiers. case_studies.summary: Jeves-style decision models give a clear choice from a set of options, useful for automated actions. The paper shows that many large language models (LLMs) can already do this without extra training, and offers a simple framework – LLM2Jev – to extract calibrated decisions from the model’s token probabilities. If you need reliable, action‑ready decisions from an LLM, this method lets you use the model as is or fine‑tune it with minimal effort, improving accuracy and trust in automated workflows.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, here is what to do: 1. Identify a decision point in your system that needs a categorical outcome (e.g., scaling decision, alert routing). 2. Use LLM2Jev to wrap a pre‑trained LLM and extract the probability distribution over your options directly from token logits. 3. If the default calibration isn’t sufficient, fine‑tune the model with a small, task‑specific dataset using LLM2Jev’s objective to improve precision. This gives you an out‑of‑the‑box, low‑maintenance decision engine for your automation pipelines.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper uncovers that general-purpose LLMs can function as Jev-style decision models without fine-tuning, offering a training-free inference recipe. This insight is novel for IT engineers who need decision outputs for automation and policy enforcement. It directly impacts IT workflows involving LLM APIs, agentic systems, and MLOps by providing a ready-to-use framework that can be integrated into existing pipelines. The framework is actionable: engineers can adopt it within 90 days to replace or augment current decision engines, improve automation, or reduce operational costs. Thus it scores high on all three criteria and does not meet the low‐signal threshold.
